topics: 🫒 Oil for a Sore Throat — olive oil in anigeron is medicine, yet pleasure still demands a blessing
🌾 Wheat Flour and Barley Flour — Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Naḥman; a raw material 'with further enhancement ahead' gets shehakol
🌴 Heart of Palm (Kura) — Rav Yehuda vs. Shmuel: is something people never plant for really a fruit?
🌿 The Caper-Bush and Orla — Rav: throw away the berries, eat the buds; Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Eliezer; leniency outside the Land
🛡️ What Counts as 'Protection for the Fruit'? — Rava's three definitions and the pomegranate experiment

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Borderline Foods
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 36a–36b
overview.hebrewSource: כֵּיוָן דְּאִית לֵיהּ הֲנָאָה מִינֵּיהּ — בָּעֵי בָּרוֹכֵי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: This daf is a parade of hard cases. Olive oil swallowed in beet water for a sore throat, plain flour, the soft heart of a young palm, the leaves and buds of a caper-bush, dry peppers and ginger, a pot of pounded grain sweetened with honey: for each, the Amoraim argue which blessing fits, or whether any is needed. Two principles keep surfacing. First, wherever a person derives pleasure, a blessing is required, even if his motive was medicinal. Second, what people plant a tree for decides whether a part of it is a fruit. The caper-bush pulls the discussion into the laws of orla, where Rava works through three definitions of 'protection for the fruit' before an experiment settles the matter.

slides.title: 🧾 The Daf's Rulings at a Glance
slides.subtitle: Each row hides a dispute; the later slides unpack the reasoning
rows: Olive oil in anigeron (beet water)
Anigeron is primary, oil secondary — unless he has a sore throat and adds much oil
בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ; medicine still needs a blessing because he enjoys it
Wheat flour
Rav Yehuda: ha'adama; Rav Naḥman: shehakol
Shehakol — flour has 'further enhancement' ahead (bread), unlike finished oil
Barley flour
Shmuel (via R' Zeira, Rav Mattana): shehakol
Taught separately lest one think it harms (worms) and needs no blessing
Heart of palm (kura)
Rav Yehuda: ha'adama, 'it is a fruit'; Shmuel: shehakol, 'it will harden'
Halakha like Shmuel — no one plants a palm for its heart
Caper: leaves, fronds / berries / buds
Mishna: leaves & fronds ha'adama; berries & buds ha'etz
Buds are not 'fruit' for orla, so for blessings too: ha'adama
Peppers / ginger
Rav Sheshet: shehakol; Rava: nothing (dry). Rava: fresh Indian ginger — ha'adama
Fresh: a blessing; dry: none, and chewing on Yom Kippur is exempt
Ḥavitz kedera / daysa
Rav Yehuda: shehakol (honey primary); Rav Kahana: mezonot (grain primary)
Rav Yosef: Rav Kahana is right — anything containing the five grains is mezonot

slides.title: 🌴 Heart of Palm: Is It a Fruit?
slides.subtitle: Shmuel compliments his student, then the Gemara sides against the student

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה — it is a fruit.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיֶה בִּדְבָרוֹ — since it will ultimately harden into the tree.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Shinnana! Your view is the reasonable one: a radish also hardens eventually, yet we say ha'adama over it.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Not so. People plant a radish for the soft radish; nobody plants a palm for its heart.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: Then anything not planted for that purpose gets no proper blessing? The caper-bush is planted for its fruit, yet the mishna gives ha'adama over its leaves and young fronds!

lines.speaker: R' Naḥman b.Y.
lines.text: People do plant a caper-bush with its leaves in mind; nobody plants a palm with its heart in mind. Although Shmuel praised Rav Yehuda, the halakha follows Shmuel.

callout.label: The test:
callout.text: A part of a plant is 'fruit' for blessing purposes when people cultivate the plant with that part in mind — נָטְעִי אִינָשֵׁי אַדַּעְתָּא.

slides.title: 🌿 Rav on the Caper-Bush: Why Not Just Say 'Halakha Like Rabbi Akiva'?
slides.subtitle: Every extra word in Rav's ruling turns out to be load-bearing

nodes.content: 📜 Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: an orla caper-bush outside Eretz Yisrael — throw away the berries (אֲבִיּוֹנוֹת) and eat the buds (קַפְרֵיסִין)
❓ So berries are fruit and buds are not? But the mishna says ha'etz over both berries and buds!
💡 Rav follows Rabbi Akiva: R' Eliezer tithes fronds, berries and buds; R' Akiva tithes only the berries, 'because it alone is fruit'

columns.label: Say 'halakha like R' Akiva'?
columns.content: Then one might apply it even in Eretz Yisrael. Rav teaches: whoever is lenient in the Land, the halakha follows him outside the Land — but not inside

columns.label: Say 'like R' Akiva outside the Land'?
columns.content: One might limit that to tree-tithes, which are rabbinic even in the Land, and still decree on orla, which is Torah law in the Land. Rav teaches: even for orla

nodes.content: 🧑‍⚖️ Ravina to Mar bar Rav Ashi, seen eating buds: if you follow lenient R' Akiva, follow Beit Shammai, who are more lenient still — they treat the caper as uncertain orla, and uncertain orla outside the Land is permitted
✅ Answer: Rabbi Akiva against Rabbi Eliezer — we follow him. Beit Shammai against Beit Hillel — 'it is not a mishna' at all

callout.label: Beit Shammai's oddity:
callout.text: They call the caper-bush a diverse kind in a vineyard (a vegetable) yet obligated in orla (a tree). The Gemara explains: they are uncertain, and rule stringently in both directions.

slides.title: 🛡️ Rava's Three Attempts to Define 'Protection for the Fruit'
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 19:23 'et piryo' includes what is secondary to the fruit — so why are caper buds permitted?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava: a 'shomer' must exist both while attached and after picking; the caper bud falls off when picked. Abaye objects: a pomegranate flower does not join the fruit for impurity, yet rinds, flower, nutshells and pits are all obligated in orla — the criteria differ
2️⃣ Rava: a 'shomer' must still be present when the fruit ripens; the bud drops earlier. Objection: Rav Naḥman in Rabba bar Avuh's name forbids orla date-coverings, which protect only the young fruit

3️⃣ Deflection: Rav Naḥman follows Rabbi Yosei, who calls even the grape-bud (סְמָדַר) a fruit. Rav Shimi of Neharde'a: but in the Sabbatical-year mishna even the Rabbis forbid cutting 'all other trees from when fruit emerges'
4️⃣ Rava, finally: a 'shomer' is something whose removal kills the fruit. Remove a caper bud and the fruit lives
5️⃣ The experiment: they removed a pomegranate's flower and it withered; they removed the caper's flower and the fruit survived
6️⃣ Halakha like Mar bar Rav Ashi: discard the berries, eat the buds. Since buds are not fruit for orla, they are not fruit for blessings either — בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה, not ha'etz

callout.label: Rav Asi's gloss:
callout.text: Beit Hillel's 'vines from when they yegaru' means the unripe grape the size of a white bean — a stage the Rabbis count as fruit, unlike the earlier grape-bud.

slides.title: 🌶️ Three Late Disputes: Peppers, Ginger, and Sweetened Grain
slides.subtitle: Two are resolved by 'fresh vs. dry', the third by Rav and Shmuel's rule

boxes.title: Peppers
items: Rava: no blessing at all — consistent with his ruling that chewing peppers on Yom Kippur is exempt
Objection: Rabbi Meir reads 'any tree for food' to include the pepper tree, whose wood tastes like its fruit — proof that Eretz Yisrael 'lacks nothing' (Deut. 8:9)
Resolution: fresh peppers are food; dry ones are not

boxes.title: Ginger
items: Rava: chewing ginger on Yom Kippur is exempt
The Sages to Mareimar: but Rava himself permits Indian ginger and rules ha'adama over it!
Same resolution: fresh ginger gets ha'adama; dry gets nothing

boxes.title: Ḥavitz Kedera / Daysa
items: Mixed with honey: Rav Yehuda says shehakol — the honey is primary; Rav Kahana says mezonot — the grain is primary
Rav Yosef: Rav Kahana is right, for Rav and Shmuel said כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מֵחֲמֵשֶׁת הַמִּינִין — anything containing the five grains — is mezonot

callout.label: Why two statements?
callout.text: Rav and Shmuel said both 'anything that has of the five grains' and 'anything that is of the five grains'. Had they said only the second, one might think mixtures are excluded; the daf ends mid-explanation of why the first is needed too.

summary.principle: Where there is pleasure there is a blessing, even for medicine; and whether a plant part is a 'fruit' depends on what people cultivate it for — a test that decides both orla and the blessing.

flowSteps.content: 🫒 Olive oil counts only in anigeron for a sore throat → ha'etz; lesson: medicine that gives pleasure needs a blessing
🌾 Flour → shehakol (further enhancement ahead); barley flour taught separately (harmful, yet enjoyed)
❓ Heart of palm: fruit or tree? Halakha like Shmuel — shehakol — because no one plants a palm for it

columns.content: 🌿 Caper orla outside the Land: Rav follows R' Akiva; buds are not 'protection' since the fruit survives without them → ha'adama on buds
🌶️ Peppers & ginger: fresh = food with a blessing, dry = nothing; ḥavitz → mezonot (Rav Kahana, Rav Yosef)

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Anything containing the five species of grain gets borei minei mezonot (Rav and Shmuel)

quiz.q: In what case does the Gemara finally locate Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that one recites 'Who creates fruit of the tree' over olive oil?
o: When one drinks the oil plain
When one dips bread into the oil
When one with a sore throat swallows a large amount of oil mixed into anigeron
When the oil is used to anoint the body
quiz.e: Drinking oil plain is harmful, and with bread the bread is primary. Only when a person with a sore throat adds much oil to anigeron is the oil primary, and despite the medicinal intent he blesses because he derives pleasure.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject Rava's comparison of wheat flour to olive oil?
o: Because flour is not eaten by anyone
Because oil is a finished product, while flour still has further enhancement ahead as bread
Because flour comes from the ground and oil from a tree
Because Rav Naḥman was Rava's teacher
quiz.e: Olive oil has no further enhancement, so it keeps the olive's blessing. Flour is a raw material on its way to bread, so neither the wheat blessing nor the bread blessing fits, and one says shehakol.

quiz.q: Why is the halakha in accordance with Shmuel that one recites shehakol over the heart of palm, even though Shmuel praised Rav Yehuda's view?
o: Because the heart of palm is harmful like barley flour
Because it ultimately hardens, just like a radish
Because people do not plant palm trees with the heart of palm in mind, unlike radishes or caper leaves
Because Shmuel retracted his praise
quiz.e: The decisive test is what people plant for. A radish is planted for the soft radish and a caper for its leaves, but no one plants a palm for its heart, so it is not a fruit.

quiz.q: What is Rava's final definition of a 'protection for the fruit' (shomer lapri) that is included in orla?
o: Anything that exists both while attached and after picking
Anything present when the fruit is fully ripe
Anything that joins the fruit for the laws of ritual impurity
Anything whose removal causes the fruit to die
quiz.e: The first two definitions were refuted by the pomegranate flower and the date coverings. Rava concludes that a shomer is that whose removal kills the fruit, confirmed by the experiment in which the pomegranate withered but the caper survived.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile Rava's ruling that chewing peppers on Yom Kippur is exempt with Rabbi Meir's teaching that the pepper tree is a 'tree for food' obligated in orla?
o: Rabbi Meir refers to fresh peppers; Rava refers to dry peppers
Rabbi Meir refers to peppers in Eretz Yisrael only
Rava retracted in favor of Rav Sheshet
Rabbi Meir refers to the wood of the tree, not its fruit
quiz.e: Fresh, damp peppers are food and are obligated in orla; dry peppers are not considered eating, so chewing them on Yom Kippur is exempt and no blessing is recited. The same distinction resolves the question about ginger.
